A.explanation: With air resistance negligible there is no work done against drag, so kinetic energy is only exchanged with gravitational potential energy and the sum $E_k + E_p$ stays constant.

B.explanation: Momentum $p = mv$ changes because gravity gives a constant downward force, so velocity and momentum change in magnitude and direction.

C.explanation: At greatest height the velocity is momentarily zero, so $E_k = \frac{1}{2}mv^2 = 0$ is minimum while $E_p = mgh$ is maximum.

D.explanation: During ascent the ball slows down, so height gained per second decreases and $E_p = mgh$ increases more slowly with time, not at a constant rate.

hints: Notice the ball is thrown vertically upwards and air resistance is negligible, so the only force doing work is weight.
Think about how $E_k = \frac{1}{2}mv^2$ and $E_p = mgh$ change as speed decreases to zero at the top and then increases on the way down.
Check whether momentum can be conserved for the ball alone when an external gravitational force acts on it throughout the flight.
walkthrough: Identify the system: a ball moving up then down with only weight acting, since air resistance is negligible and there is no contact force after release.
State the energy rule: with no dissipative work, mechanical energy is conserved, so loss of kinetic energy equals gain of gravitational potential energy and $E_k + E_p = \text{constant}$.
Apply to the motion: on ascent $v$ decreases so $E_k$ decreases while $h$ increases so $E_p$ increases; on descent the reverse happens, but the total stays the same.
Reject the momentum idea: conservation of momentum needs no resultant external force, but weight $mg$ acts all the time, so $p = mv$ is not constant.
Reject the other statements: $E_k$ is zero, not greatest, at maximum $h$, and $E_p$ does not grow linearly with time because the upward speed is decreasing. This is option A.
